item.content:encoded:

NVIDIA Stocks Slide 4.43% as Report Alleges $7.5 Billion in Chips Reached China 1 min read

NVDA NVIDIA NVDA shares fell 4.43% to $170.75 as of 9:53 a.m. ET in regular trading on November 10, after The Information reported that Jensen Huang's personal relationship with a businesswoman alleged to work for Beijing helped move at least $7.5 billion of its chips to Chinese firms. That stacks on Monday's 4.27% drop. Reuters, which carried the report, said it could not independently verify the claims. The report describes a web of companies in China and Singapore, centered on Shanghai Century Litong, that won preferred cloud-partner status within months of its June 2023 founding. When orders for export-restricted chips stalled, roughly 240,000 H100, H200 and A100 units allegedly reached China. Some of that capacity reportedly served Alibaba, Tencent and smaller Chinese AI labs. The company's board said a committee of independent directors with outside counsel is running the review. The board added that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

From the November 6 close of $186.64, the two-day slide is 8.51%, roughly $383 billion of market value on about 24.1 billion shares. The GuruFocus profile is lopsided: GF Score 92/100, Profitability 10/10, Financial Strength 9/10 and Momentum 10/10, but GF Value Rank only 2/10. At $170.75 the shares trade 60.10% below the $427.93 GF Value, yet GuruFocus itself tags the setup "Possible Value Trap, Think Twice." The model gap alone is no bargain signal. The next hard test is the November 17 third-quarter report, where any export-control questions would surface in guidance or disclosures.

item.content:encoded:
News / GuruFocus / Nvidia Stock Plunges Despite President Trump Backs Huang in China Spy Storm

Nvidia Stock Plunges Despite President Trump Backs Huang in China Spy Storm Less than 1 min read

NVDA Nvidia NVDA shares fell about 3% on Tuesday despite President Donald Trump voicing support for CEO Jensen Huang amid an internal company investigation involving allegations of Chinese espionage. Trump said Monday that he had spoken with Huang and believed the executive was unaware of the alleged intelligence links of a woman connected to him. The president also confirmed that the FBI was examining the matter. Huang acknowledged the relationship in an email to employees Sunday and pledged to cooperate with Nvidia's investigation, according to media reports. The woman, identified as Alice Huang, is suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of attempting to influence the chipmaker's position on restrictions governing advanced semiconductor exports to China. Elon Musk and investor Bill Ackman (Trades, Portfolio) have also publicly backed Huang, while Nvidia has maintained that it has no reason to believe company trade secrets or U.S. national security information were compromised. China has rejected the espionage claims, describing them as unfounded. The controversy has also drawn legal scrutiny. Nvidia and Huang were sued by shareholders in a proposed class-action case filed in California, with investors alleging that they were not informed about potential risks associated with the matter.

Dan Ives Says Microsoft Amazon and Meta Win Big as Data Center Slowdown Looms Less than 1 min read

SPCX TSLA AMZN Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said a potential slowdown in U.S. data center construction could favor major cloud providers with operating capacity, according to a Monday research note. He cited midterm election results and Texas governor Gina Hinojosa's approach to data center development, where SpaceX SPCX and Tesla TSLA have large operations. Ives estimated that 10% to 30% of planned U.S. data centers may not be built over the next 18 months under a "Blue Wave" scenario. He said firms with available gigawatts and GPUs could become more valuable. The note named Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon AMZN , Alphabet (GOOGL), Meta Platforms (META), and in some cases Oracle (ORCL) as potential beneficiaries. Overall capital spending is still expected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion over the next few years, with Big Tech capex above $1 trillion next year, Ives said. A slower buildout could reduce capital raising by about 25% over the next year. Ives added that the AI revolution will continue, though at a slower rate, and political leaders will need to balance data center concerns with global AI competition.
